chapter.name: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical

questions.q: True or False? Give the reason or the correction. 'Crushing a piece of chalk into powder is a chemical change, because the chalk piece cannot be got back from the powder.'
questions.a: False. The chalk is still chalk; only its size has changed and no new substance forms. Not being able to undo a change does not make it chemical.
s: verdict: false
reason: only size changes, no new substance, so reversibility is not the test

questions.q: A student heats a white powder in a test tube and notes four observations. Which one, on its own, shows that a chemical change took place?
questions.a: A gas that turns lime water milky is carbon dioxide, a new substance. Melting and setting is a change of state, and finer grains or pellets are changes of size or shape, all physical.
o: The gas given off turns freshly prepared lime water milky
Some of the powder melts into a liquid that sets again on cooling
The lumps in the powder break into finer grains when pressed
The powder is shaped into small pellets with a spatula

questions.q: In a village kitchen water boils in a pot over a wood fire, and the wood under the pot keeps burning. Which statement about the two changes is correct?
questions.a: Boiling only changes the state of water, so it is physical. Burning wood forms new substances, so it is chemical. Heat as a cause does not decide the type.
o: Boiling is physical (still water); burning wood is chemical (new substance)
Both are physical, because heat is the cause of each change here
Both are chemical, because each one needs a flame and gives something out
Boiling is chemical as a gas forms; burning is physical as the wood just shrinks

questions.q: An inflated balloon is pricked with a pin and bursts. Raju says a new substance has formed. Which finding would support his claim?
questions.a: Only a material with properties different from rubber would show a new substance. Change of shape or size, escape of air or inability to undo the change do not show it.
o: The torn pieces turn out to have properties different from rubber
The pieces cannot be joined together again to get the inflated balloon back
The burst balloon now has a very different shape and size from before
The air that was inside the balloon has escaped into the room

questions.q: Two wet towels are hung out, one in shade and one in sun. By evening the sunny towel is dry. Ritu says the sunny towel has undergone a chemical change because it has lost its water. What is the correct reply?
questions.a: Drying changes liquid water to gas (vapour), which is still water. The cotton is unchanged, so no new substance forms and the change is physical.
o: Only the water's state changed (liquid to gas); no new substance forms
The cotton lost its water and so became a new material, which makes Ritu right
A gas forms from the water, and a gas is always a new substance
Sunlight takes part in the change, and any change needing sunlight is chemical

questions.q:
Read the statements about physical changes.
I. Folding a sheet of paper into a boat changes its shape, but the material is still paper.
II. When liquid water becomes a gas, the gas is a different substance from water.
III. A change in which only shape, size or state alters, with no new substance, is a physical change.
questions.a: II is false: a change of state does not make a new substance, so water vapour is still water. I and III are true.
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A change in which an object's size and shape alter beyond recognition must be a chemical change.
Reason (R): A chemical change is recognised by the formation of a new substance, not by how different the object looks.
questions.a: A is false: crushing chalk or folding paper alters appearance a great deal and is still physical. R is true and is exactly why A fails.
o: Assertion is false, but the Reason is true
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Assertion is true, but the Reason is false

questions.q: A 5 cm stick of chalk is crushed into fine powder and every grain is collected. The number of new substances present in the powder is ___.

Match Column I with Column II.
1. Wet bibs on a rope are dry by evening
2. A paper strip is folded into a boat
3. A wooden splint is lit and leaves a black solid
4. A chalk stick is ground into rangoli powder
A. Only the size changes; the chalk is still chalk
B. New substances form along with heat and light
C. Water changes its state from liquid to gas
D. Only the shape changes; the paper is still paper
questions.a: Drying: liquid water to gas (C); folded paper: shape only (D); burning splint: new substances (B); ground chalk: size only (A).

questions.q:
A cube of ice in a steel tumbler becomes water on a classroom table. The tumbler is then left on a hot terrace until it is dry.
(a) Name the state of water at the start and at the end.
(b) A student says the water at the end is not the same substance as the ice at the start because it looks different. Answer her with the chapter's test.
questions.a: (a) Solid (ice) at the start; gas (water vapour) at the end. (b) At each step only the state changed and no new substance formed, so it is still the same substance, water.
s: solid at the start and gas at the end
only the state changed, no new substance, same substance

questions.q:
Sunita cuts a paper strip into pieces, folds one piece into a boat and then lights the boat with a match.
(a) At which step does the change stop being physical?
(b) Say how what is left after cutting differs from what is left after lighting.
questions.a: (a) At the lighting; cutting and folding change only size and shape. (b) The cut pieces are still paper; lighting forms new substances, so the product is no longer paper.
s: lighting is the step where the change turns chemical
pieces are still paper but lighting gives new substances

questions.q:
Tanvi sees that a banana on the shelf has more brown spots and a stronger smell today than yesterday, and says, 'My eyes and nose are enough to name the type of change.'
(a) Which two senses did she use?
(b) Say what her senses can tell her and what question she must still ask.
questions.a: (a) Sight (brown spots) and smell (stronger smell). (b) The senses show that some property has changed; to name the type of change she must ask whether a new substance has formed.
s: sight and smell
senses show a change; the new-substance question names the type

questions.q:
Hari boils water in a pan until half of it is gone. He then holds a cold steel plate over the steam.
(a) Where has the missing water gone?
(b) What will he see on the plate, and what does it show about the change?
questions.a: (a) It has become water vapour (gas) and mixed with the air. (b) Droplets of water collect on the plate; the vapour turns back into water, so the change is a change of state and no new substance formed.
s: missing water is now vapour in the air
droplets of water show same substance, physical change

questions.q: Isha says: 'A change is physical when only the shape or size of an object changes.' Is she right? Comment on how complete her statement is.
questions.a: Partly right. Shape and size changes are physical, but she left out change of state (melting, boiling, drying), which is also physical. What really defines a physical change is that no new substance is formed.
s: verdict: partly right
what is missing: change of state
the real test: no new substance is formed

questions.q: Describe a situation at school or home in which one object first goes through a physical change and then through a chemical change. Label each and give a reason.
questions.a: e.g. A log is chopped into splinters (physical: size and shape only) and a splinter is then burnt (chemical: new substances form with heat and light).
s: situation with the two changes in order
physical change labelled with reason
chemical change labelled with reason

questions.q: Neha claims that melting ice makes a new substance because ice and water look so different. Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: A new substance would have to differ in more than looks. Melting changes only the state, solid to liquid, and water in either state is the same substance, so it is a physical change.
s: what a new substance would require
melting is only a change of state
conclusion: same substance, physical

questions.q:
Your class runs a 'Physical or not?' stall at the science exhibition. Visitors pick a card and sort it. The cards are: folding a paper boat, an ice cube melting in the sun, lighting a wooden splint, crushing a chalk stick.
(a) Write the one question every visitor should ask of each card.
(b) Use it to sort the four cards.
(c) Name the card most likely to fool a visitor who judges by how different the product looks, and say why the test does not fool.
(d) Write one line for the board telling visitors what not to rely on.
questions.a: (a) Is a new substance formed? (b) Boat, melting ice and crushed chalk are physical; the lit splint is chemical. (c) Melting ice: the water looks very different from ice but is the same substance in another state. (d) Do not decide by how different the thing looks.
s: the test question: is a new substance formed
correct sort: three physical, the splint chemical
melting ice as the misleading card with reason
advice not to judge by looks alone

questions.q:
A student's test answer reads: 'Boiling water is chemical because bubbles appear and a gas forms. Crushing chalk is chemical because it cannot be undone. Burning wood is physical because the wood only becomes smaller.'
(a) Mark each sentence right or wrong and correct it.
(b) Name the one test all three corrections rest on.
(c) Write a one-line rule that would have prevented all three errors.
questions.a: Boiling water is physical (only the state changes). Crushing chalk is physical (same chalk, smaller). Burning wood is chemical (new substances form). All rest on: is a new substance formed? Rule: decide by new substance, not by bubbles, reversibility or size.
s: boiling water corrected to physical, state change
crushing chalk corrected to physical, size change
burning wood corrected to chemical, new substances
the test: is a new substance formed
rule that ignores bubbles, reversibility and size

questions.q:
On Sports Day the canteen team does four jobs. Job 1: twelve ice cubes are put in a bucket of water and have melted by the end of the first race. Job 2: thirty oranges are chopped for the interval. Job 3: wood is lit under a pot and the water in the pot boils for tea. Job 4: wet bibs hung on a rope are dry by lunch. The head wants a list of jobs for Class 6 volunteers, limited to jobs in which no new substance forms.
(a) For Jobs 1 and 4, name the state of water before and after.
(b) Which property of the oranges changes in Job 2?
(c) In Job 3, which of the two changes forms new substances?
(d) Decide which jobs go on the volunteers' list and justify.
questions.a: (a) Job 1 solid to liquid; Job 4 liquid to gas. (b) Size and shape. (c) The burning of the wood. (d) Jobs 1, 2 and 4: they are physical. Job 3 includes burning, a chemical change, so it stays off the list.
s: states: solid to liquid and liquid to gas
oranges change in size and shape
burning wood forms new substances, boiling does not
list of Jobs 1, 2 and 4 with reason

questions.q:
At a Diwali mela, Bela runs three stalls. At the rangoli stall chalk sticks are ground into coloured powder. At the balloon stall a child pricks an inflated balloon to win a prize. At the gola stall a block of ice is crushed and the crushed ice slowly turns to water. Bela's poster says, 'Every change at our three stalls is physical.' In the evening the stalls are lit by cotton wicks burning in oil in diyas.
(a) What changes about the chalk and what stays the same?
(b) What is true of the rubber of the burst balloon?
(c) At the gola stall name the change of size and then the change of state, in order.
(d) Decide whether the poster is correct once the diyas are counted, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Its size changes; it is still chalk. (b) It is still rubber; only shape and size changed. (c) Crushing (size), then melting (solid to liquid). (d) Not correct: burning of the wick and oil forms new substances, a chemical change.
s: size changes, chalk stays chalk
rubber is still rubber
crushing then melting in order
poster wrong because burning is chemical

questions.q: To show that the gas from vinegar and baking soda is carbon dioxide, Veena says, 'Watch whether it bubbles in water.' Wasim says, 'Pass it through freshly prepared lime water.' Whose test works, and why?
questions.a: Exhaled air gives only bubbles in tap water, so bubbling does not identify a gas. The milkiness of lime water is the test for carbon dioxide.
o: Wasim's: bubbles also show in tap water, but milky lime water signals carbon dioxide
Veena's: bubbles rising through water show that the gas is carbon dioxide itself
Both work equally well, since any gas that bubbles through a liquid is carbon dioxide
Neither works, as only the fizzing sound at the first mixture shows which gas formed

questions.q: Nisha has two unlabelled cups of clear liquid, one holding tap water and the other lime water. She blows exhaled air into each through a separate straw, one at a time. Which finding lets her tell the cups apart?
questions.a: Bubbles appear in both cups. Only lime water turns milky, as carbon dioxide from the breath reacts with it.
o: Only one cup turns milky, and it is the lime water
Only one cup shows bubbles, and it is the lime water
Only one cup gives out a smell, and it is the tap water
Only one cup becomes warm, and it is the lime water

questions.q: A reaction is written: Calcium hydroxide + Carbon dioxide gives Calcium carbonate + Water. Which pair names one reactant and one product, in that order?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide is on the reactant side and calcium carbonate on the product side. The pair with water first, or with both substances being products, does not fit.
o: Carbon dioxide; calcium carbonate
Calcium carbonate; calcium hydroxide
Water; calcium hydroxide
Calcium carbonate; water

questions.q: Freshly prepared lime water is poured into three clean tumblers. P: exhaled air is blown in through a straw. Q: gas from lemon juice and baking soda is passed in. R: the lime water is only stirred with a clean spoon. In which tumblers does a chemical change take place?
questions.a: In P and Q carbon dioxide reacts with lime water and a new white substance forms. Stirring in R changes nothing but the movement of the liquid.
o: P and Q only
P only
Q and R only
P, Q and R

questions.q:
Read the statements about the lime water test.
I. Bubbles rising when exhaled air is blown into a liquid show that carbon dioxide has reacted.
II. A white substance that does not dissolve in water, calcium carbonate, is formed.
III. A small amount of water is also formed in the reaction.
questions.a: I is false: tap water also bubbles and stays clear. II and III are true.
o: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Freshly prepared lime water turns milky when the gas from vinegar and baking soda is passed through it.
Reason (R): The gas formed is carbon dioxide, which reacts with the calcium hydroxide in lime water.
questions.a: Both are true. The reaction of carbon dioxide with calcium hydroxide forms the milky calcium carbonate, so R explains A.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

questions.q: Six cups hold equal amounts of lime water. Exhaled air is blown into 2 cups, gas from vinegar and baking soda is passed into 3 cups, and the last cup is left untouched. The number of cups that turn milky is ___.

Match Column I with Column II.
1. Exhaled air is blown into tap water
2. Gas from lemon juice and baking soda goes into lime water
3. Milky lime water is left undisturbed for some time
4. The change in lime water is written as a chemical equation
A. A white insoluble substance settles at the bottom
B. Calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide gives calcium carbonate + water
C. Bubbles appear, with no change in appearance of the water
D. The lime water turns milky, showing carbon dioxide
questions.a: Tap water: bubbles only (C); gas into lime water: milky (D); standing: a white layer settles (A); equation (B).

questions.q: True or False? Give the reason or the correction. 'Because exhaled air and the gas from vinegar with baking soda both turn lime water milky, the test shows the gas in both is carbon dioxide but cannot show where the gas came from.'
questions.a: True. The milkiness identifies the gas, carbon dioxide, whatever its source. Telling the breath from the vinegar mixture needs knowing how the gas was made.
s: verdict: true
reason: the test identifies the gas, not its source

questions.q:
Anita passes the gas from lemon juice and baking soda into a second bottle holding tap water. She sees bubbles and says, 'There is no carbon dioxide, as nothing changed in the water.'
(a) What is wrong with her set-up?
(b) What should the second bottle hold, and what result would she then expect?
questions.a: (a) Tap water only bubbles with a gas and cannot show carbon dioxide. (b) Freshly prepared lime water, which would turn milky if the gas is carbon dioxide.
s: tap water cannot detect carbon dioxide, so her conclusion fails
freshly prepared lime water that turns milky

questions.q:
Lemon juice and baking soda are mixed in a small bottle.
(a) Write the word equation for the change in the bottle.
(b) Give two observations that show a new substance has formed.
questions.a: (a) Lemon juice (or vinegar) + baking soda gives carbon dioxide + other substances. (b) A fizzing sound with gas bubbles, and the gas turns lime water milky.
s: word equation giving carbon dioxide and other substances
fizzing with bubbles, and milky lime water

questions.q:
Zeba blows into lime water; the tumbler turns milky at once. After an hour the liquid is clearer and a white layer lies at the bottom.
(a) What has happened to the white particles?
(b) Why does this show that they are not dissolved?
questions.a: (a) They have settled down to the bottom. (b) Calcium carbonate is insoluble in water; a dissolved substance would stay spread through the liquid and not settle.
s: particles settled at the bottom
insoluble calcium carbonate does not stay dissolved

questions.q:
Zeba says the change in lime water and the change in the vinegar and baking soda bottle are the same kind of change though the substances differ.
(a) Name that kind of change.
(b) Name the new substance that shows it in each case.
questions.a: (a) Chemical change. (b) In the bottle, carbon dioxide forms; in the lime water, calcium carbonate (white and insoluble) forms.
s: chemical change
carbon dioxide in one, calcium carbonate in the other

questions.q: Bela says: 'Lime water turns milky because bubbles of exhaled air get trapped in it, and the white layer next morning is just those bubbles settling.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. Tap water also gets bubbles from the same breath and stays clear. In lime water the carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide to form calcium carbonate, a white solid that does not dissolve and so settles.
s: verdict: no
tap water bubbles but stays clear
milkiness and layer are calcium carbonate, a new substance

questions.q: Write a three-line lab note of an investigation whose conclusion is 'a chemical change took place in cup B but not in cup A'. Include what each cup held and what was seen.
questions.a: e.g. Cup A held tap water and cup B lime water; the same breath was blown into each through a separate straw. A showed bubbles only; B showed bubbles and turned milky. A new substance formed in B only, so the chemical change took place there.
s: what each cup held and how the test was done
the observation in each cup
conclusion tied to a new substance forming in B

questions.q: A student plans to prove that the gas from vinegar and baking soda is carbon dioxide using only the fizzing sound. Show why this evidence alone cannot prove it.
questions.a: Fizzing and bubbles only show that some gas is being formed. The gas is identified as carbon dioxide only when it is passed through freshly prepared lime water and turns it milky.
s: fizzing shows only that a gas forms
the gas is not identified by sound or bubbles
lime water turning milky is the test that identifies it

questions.q:
A class records three tumblers. T1: tap water, exhaled air blown in: bubbles only. T2: lime water, exhaled air blown in: bubbles, milky, and a white layer an hour later. T3: lime water, gas from vinegar and baking soda passed in: milky.
(a) State what T1 and T2 together show.
(b) State what T3 adds and name the gas in T3.
(c) Write the word equation for the change in T2.
(d) A student says T1 is a waste of time. Decide, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) Bubbles alone are not a chemical change; the milkiness in T2 is a new substance. (b) T3 shows the gas from vinegar and baking soda also turns lime water milky, so it is carbon dioxide. (c) Calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide gives calcium carbonate + water. (d) T1 is needed: it is the comparison that shows bubbles appear without any chemical change.
s: T1 and T2 together: bubbles are not the evidence, milkiness is
T3: the gas is carbon dioxide
word equation of the lime water change
T1 is the comparison that separates bubbles from milkiness

questions.q:
Two plans for showing carbon dioxide to a class. Plan X: students blow exhaled air through a separate straw into lime water. Plan Y: vinegar and baking soda are mixed in one bottle and the gas is led by a flexible straw into a second bottle of lime water.
(a) Name the gas and its source in each plan.
(b) State what is seen at the end of each plan.
(c) Name the caution from the activity that applies to Plan X.
(d) A student in the class has a bad cold. Decide which plan the teacher should use and justify.
questions.a: (a) Both give carbon dioxide: from the breath in X, from the reaction of vinegar and baking soda in Y. (b) The lime water turns milky in both. (c) Do not suck the water or lime water through the straw. (d) Plan Y: nobody has to blow into the straw, and the same result is seen.
s: carbon dioxide from the breath in X and from the reaction in Y
lime water turns milky in both
caution: do not suck the lime water
Plan Y chosen because nobody blows into the straw

questions.q:
The science club will show carbon dioxide to 200 visitors in batches of 40. Plan X: each visitor blows into lime water through his own straw; straws come in packs of 50 for Rs 20, and lime water for the day costs Rs 25. Plan Y: each batch sees a fresh vinegar and baking soda demonstration costing Rs 14, with the same Rs 25 of lime water for the day. The principal allows a total spend of at most Rs 100.
(a) Name the gas shown by each plan and what it reacts with.
(b) What shows in Plan Y that the gas is the same one as in Plan X?
(c) Work out the total cost of each plan.
(d) Decide which plan the club should run and name one precaution.
questions.a: (a) Carbon dioxide, reacting with calcium hydroxide in lime water. (b) The lime water turns milky in both. (c) X: 4 packs x Rs 20 + Rs 25 = Rs 105. Y: 5 batches x Rs 14 + Rs 25 = Rs 95. (d) Plan Y, as only it stays within Rs 100; precaution: adult supervision and never suck the lime water.
s: carbon dioxide reacting with calcium hydroxide
lime water turns milky in both plans
X Rs 105 and Y Rs 95
Plan Y within the budget, with a precaution

questions.q:
At a camp, Jaya lit a candle in a petri dish and covered it with a tumbler. After the flame went out she poured a little freshly prepared lime water into the dish, swirled it, and it turned milky. Her brother Tej says, 'This proves the candle used up all the air under the tumbler.'
(a) What does the milkiness show about the gas under the tumbler?
(b) Where did the carbon and the oxygen in that gas come from?
(c) Is the formation of this gas a physical or a chemical change? Give a reason.
(d) Decide whether Tej's claim is supported by what the activity shows.
questions.a: (a) It contains carbon dioxide. (b) Carbon from the wax and oxygen from the air. (c) Chemical: a new substance forms. (d) Not supported: the test shows carbon dioxide formed and the flame stopped as the supply of air (its oxygen) was cut off; it does not show that all the air was used.
s: carbon dioxide is present
carbon from wax and oxygen from air
chemical, because a new substance forms
claim goes beyond the evidence: oxygen, not all the air

questions.q: On a garden walk at dusk, students see a firefly glowing and a lit diya on a wall. Which statement correctly compares the two lights?
questions.a: Firefly light is bioluminescence, a chemical change that gives light without heat. The diya is combustion, which gives heat with light.
o: Both lights come from chemical changes, but only the diya gives out heat with its light
Both are burning, but the firefly burns more slowly than the diya does, with a dimmer glow
The firefly light is a physical change in a living insect; the diya light is a chemical change
Both give out heat along with light, as every chemical change that makes light also makes heat

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a product when a magnesium ribbon burns in air?
questions.a: Oxygen is a reactant taken from the air. The products are magnesium oxide, heat and light.
o: Oxygen
Magnesium oxide
Heat
Light

questions.q: A brown powder rubbed off an old iron gate cannot be turned back into shiny iron. A student says, 'The gate still has its shape, so only a physical change happened.' Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Rust is a new brown substance, iron oxide. Keeping the shape of the gate does not show the absence of a new substance.
o: The brown powder is rust, iron oxide, a new substance, so the change is chemical
Iron has broken into fine pieces of itself, which is only a physical change of size
Rust is iron that has changed its state into a powder, so it is a physical change
Keeping its shape shows that no new substance has formed on the gate at all

questions.q: Zoya burns a short magnesium ribbon inside a tightly closed glass jar of air. Which prediction does the chapter support best?
questions.a: Combustion needs oxygen, and a closed jar has no continuous supply of air, so the burning stops once the oxygen in it is used.
o: It burns only until the oxygen in the jar is used up, and then stops
It burns for as long as the jar stays warm, because the heat keeps it going on
It does not burn at all inside a closed jar since there is no open flame
It burns for exactly as long as it would burn in the open air outside

questions.q: Which observation shows combustion, and not merely some other chemical change?
questions.a: Combustion is a reaction with oxygen that gives out heat and/or light. The other three changes form new substances without that heat or light.
o: A ribbon of magnesium lit in air gives light and heat and leaves white powder
Iron nails left in damp air slowly form a brown layer over many days and weeks
Lime water turns milky when exhaled air is blown into it through a straw
Vinegar fizzes and bubbles of gas form when baking soda is added to it

questions.q:
Read the statements about burning and rusting.
I. Burning a magnesium ribbon forms magnesium oxide and gives out heat and light.
II. Wood, paper, cotton and kerosene are combustible substances.
III. Any chemical reaction that gives out heat and light is combustion, even if oxygen takes no part.
questions.a: III is false: combustion is a reaction of a substance with oxygen that gives heat and/or light. I and II are true.
o: I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Synthetic cloth should never be used to put out a fire on a person.
Reason (R): Wrapping a blanket or cloth round the person cuts off the supply of air.
questions.a: Both are true. R explains why wrapping works at all, but it does not explain why synthetic cloth is banned, which is because it can melt and stick to the skin.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

questions.q: A blanket is wrapped round a person whose clothes are on fire. The gas whose supply to the flames is cut off is ___.
questions.a: oxygen

questions.q: True or False? Give the reason or the correction. 'Burning magnesium ribbon is a chemical change only because it gives out heat and light; if it gave none, it would be a physical change.'
questions.a: False. It is chemical because a new substance, magnesium oxide, forms; heat and light accompany the change but do not decide its type.
s: verdict: false
reason: the formation of magnesium oxide is the test

questions.q:
Rusting forms iron oxide and burning magnesium forms magnesium oxide.
(a) Which of the two oxides is brown and which is a white powder?
(b) Say what the two changes have in common as types of change.
questions.a: (a) Iron oxide (rust) is brown; magnesium oxide is the white powder. (b) Both are chemical changes, because in each a new substance is formed.
s: iron oxide brown, magnesium oxide white
both chemical, new substance forms

questions.q:
A notebook says: 'Bioluminescence is the light a candle gives out.'
(a) Correct the note.
(b) State one thing the two kinds of light have in common.
questions.a: (a) Bioluminescence is light produced without heat by living organisms, such as fireflies; a candle gives light along with heat by combustion. (b) Both lights are produced by chemical changes.
s: bioluminescence: light without heat in living organisms
both are produced by chemical changes

questions.q:
At a canteen, a worker's apron is on fire and a helper wraps a thin synthetic sheet tightly around her.
(a) What can go wrong with this choice of cloth?
(b) What should be used instead, and what does it do to the fire?
questions.a: (a) Synthetic cloth can melt and stick to the skin. (b) A blanket or cloth that is not synthetic, such as cotton; it cuts off the supply of air so the fire goes out.
s: synthetic cloth can melt and stick to the skin
a cotton blanket or cloth cuts off the supply of air

questions.q:
A student writes the burning of magnesium as: Magnesium oxide gives Magnesium + Oxygen + Heat + Light.
(a) Say what is wrong with it.
(b) Rewrite it correctly.
questions.a: (a) The two sides are reversed: magnesium and oxygen are the reactants and magnesium oxide is a product. (b) Magnesium + Oxygen gives Magnesium oxide + Heat + Light.
s: reactants and products are swapped
correct equation

questions.q: Mina says: 'Magnesium oxide is just the ribbon crumbled into a white powder, so burning a magnesium ribbon is a physical change.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. The powder is magnesium oxide, a new substance, formed when magnesium reacts with oxygen, and heat and light are given out. A crumbling would leave magnesium itself unchanged.
s: verdict: no
magnesium oxide is a new substance formed with oxygen
heat and light given out show the reaction; crumbling would not form a new substance

questions.q: Write a three-line home situation in which a fire is put out by cutting off the air. Name the material used, say why it is chosen and name one material you would not use.
questions.a: e.g. A cotton dupatta catches fire at a lamp. Her mother wraps a thick cotton blanket round her, which cuts off the air so the fire goes out. A synthetic sheet should not be used because it can melt and stick to the skin.
s: situation where the air supply is cut off
material named with reason
synthetic material rejected with reason

questions.q: Compare the burning of a magnesium ribbon with the glowing of a firefly in three respects.
questions.a: Both are chemical changes. Magnesium reacts with oxygen giving magnesium oxide with heat and light, which is combustion. A firefly gives light without heat in a living organism, called bioluminescence.
s: both are chemical changes
magnesium: combustion giving heat and light
firefly: light without heat, bioluminescence

questions.q:
Three groups cover identical burning candles. Group A uses no tumbler. Group B uses a 250 mL tumbler and its flame goes out after 14 s. Group C uses a 500 mL tumbler and its flame goes out after 27 s.
(a) Why does the flame in B go out?
(b) Why does C last longer than B?
(c) How would you show that carbon dioxide has formed in the tumbler of B?
(d) A student says, 'C lasted about twice as long, so the candle uses only half the air in B.' Evaluate.
questions.a: (a) The covered candle has no continuous supply of air, so its oxygen runs out. (b) The larger tumbler holds more air, hence more oxygen. (c) Add a little lime water to the dish; it turns milky. (d) Not supported: the data show that more air gives a longer flame, not how much air is used.
s: no continuous supply of air; oxygen runs out
larger tumbler holds more air and oxygen
lime water turns milky
claim goes beyond the data: only that more air lasts longer

questions.q:
Fatima's notebook has four events. P: a magnesium ribbon is lit in air; a bright light and heat are given out and a white powder remains. Q: iron nails left in damp air slowly form brown flakes; nothing glows and no heat is noticed. R: a firefly glows at night; the insect does not feel warm. S: a candle under an inverted tumbler goes out after some time.
(a) Which of P and Q is combustion, and why?
(b) Name the new substance formed in P and in Q.
(c) Name the process in R.
(d) What do P and S show about what combustion needs?
questions.a: (a) P: a substance reacts with oxygen and gives heat and light; Q gives none. (b) P: magnesium oxide; Q: rust (iron oxide). (c) Bioluminescence. (d) Both burn only with a continuous supply of oxygen: S goes out when the air supply is cut off.
s: P is combustion: reacts with oxygen with heat and light
magnesium oxide and rust
bioluminescence
combustion needs a continuous supply of oxygen

questions.q:
A hostel has three floors and needs one fire blanket for each floor. A cotton blanket costs Rs 450 and a synthetic blanket costs Rs 300. The warden's budget is Rs 1500. She knows a girl's cotton dupatta once caught fire from a lamp.
(a) Which requirement of burning does a blanket wrapped round a person remove?
(b) What does the chapter say about synthetic blankets?
(c) Work out the cost of one blanket per floor in cotton and in synthetic.
(d) Decide which kind to buy and justify.
questions.a: (a) The supply of air (oxygen). (b) A synthetic blanket should never be used, as it can melt and stick to the skin. (c) Cotton: 3 x 450 = Rs 1350; synthetic: 3 x 300 = Rs 900. (d) Cotton: Rs 1350 is within Rs 1500, so the safer kind can be bought; the Rs 450 saved by synthetic is not worth the risk.
s: the supply of air
synthetic can melt and stick to the skin
Rs 1350 and Rs 900
cotton within budget, safety over saving

questions.q:
During a power cut Meher lights a candle in a tall glass jar and puts a lid on the jar so that the evening breeze cannot blow it out. Within a short time the flame goes out. Her friend says, 'The wax must have run out.' The festival programme needs the candle to burn for an hour.
(a) Why did the flame go out?
(b) Is the friend's explanation consistent with the chapter's activity? Give a reason.
(c) Is the burning of the candle combustion? Give the reason.
(d) Decide whether Meher should keep the lid on or take it off for the hour, and justify.
questions.a: (a) The covered jar has no continuous supply of air, so the oxygen is used up. (b) No: in the activity the covered candle goes out while the uncovered one keeps burning with the same wax. (c) Yes: the wax reacts with oxygen and gives heat and light. (d) Take the lid off, or leave the top open: a continuous supply of air is needed for an hour, even though the breeze is a risk.
s: air supply cut, oxygen used up
uncovered candle keeps burning, so wax is not the reason
combustion: reaction with oxygen giving heat and light
lid off to keep air supply, with reason

questions.q: Substance X has an ignition temperature of 120 degrees C and substance Y has 300 degrees C. Both have plenty of air. A metal plate kept at 200 degrees C is held against each for a long time. What happens?
questions.a: X is heated to its ignition temperature of 120 degrees C by the 200 degree plate, so it burns. Y cannot be raised to 300 degrees C by a 200 degree plate. A flame is not needed.
o: X catches fire and Y does not
Y catches fire and X does not
Both catch fire, since both are fuels
Neither catches fire, since there is no flame

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT needed for a piece of paper to start burning?
questions.a: Paper burns under focused sunrays without any flame. Fuel, oxygen and heat to the ignition temperature are the three requirements.
o: A flame touching it
Oxygen from the air
Heat that raises it to its ignition temperature
The paper itself as a fuel

questions.q: Neha tilts her magnifying glass so that the sunrays fall on the paper as a large, faint circle instead of the smallest, brightest spot. What is the likely result?
questions.a: The smallest, brightest spot concentrates the heat. A large faint circle supplies less heat to any one place, so reaching the ignition temperature is slower or may not happen.
o: The heat is spread out, so the paper reaches its ignition temperature later or never
The paper catches fire sooner, because a bigger part of its surface is lit up and so burns
The ignition temperature of the paper rises with the size of the circle, so it cannot burn
The oxygen around the paper is cut off by the lens, so the paper cannot burn there

questions.q: A grass fire is spreading across a field. Villagers clear a wide strip of dry grass ahead of it. Which side of the fire triangle does this take away from the advancing fire?
questions.a: With no dry grass to burn in the cleared strip, the fire has no fuel there. The air is still present and the heat only matters if there is fuel.
o: Fuel
Oxygen
Heat
None, it only changes the wind

questions.q:
Read the statements about combustion.
I. A substance can catch fire only if a flame touches it.
II. If oxygen is removed from a fire, the fire stops only when the fuel is removed too.
III. Fuel, oxygen and heat that brings the fuel to its ignition temperature are all needed for combustion.
questions.a: I is false: paper burns under focused sunrays with no flame. II is false: removing any one of the three sides stops combustion. III is true.
o: III only
I only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Paper can be set on fire using a magnifying glass and sunlight.
Reason (R): Focusing the sunrays lowers the ignition temperature of the paper.
questions.a: A is true: the paper is heated until it burns. R is false: the ignition temperature does not change; the paper is heated up to it.
o: Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

questions.q: A stack of paper kept on a shelf for years never burns, though fuel and oxygen are both present. The side of the fire triangle that is missing is ___.
questions.a: heat

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
1. Paper lying on a desk for years
2. A burning candle covered by a tumbler
3. A stone held to a lighted matchstick
4. Paper under the focused sunray spot
A. The air supply is cut off
B. Fuel is missing
C. Heat reaches the ignition temperature without any flame
D. Heat to the ignition temperature is missing
questions.a: Paper on a desk: no heat to reach its ignition temperature (D); covered candle: air cut off (A); stone: no fuel (B); focused sunrays: heat without flame (C).

questions.q: True or False? Give the reason or the correction. 'Cooling a burning sheet of paper below its ignition temperature will stop the burning, even though fuel and oxygen are still present.'
questions.a: True. Heat that keeps the paper at or above its ignition temperature is one of the three requirements; taking it away breaks the fire triangle.
s: verdict: true
reason: heat is one of the three requirements, so removing it stops combustion

questions.q:
Ravi watches the magnifying glass set a sheet on fire and says, 'The lens has made fire out of nothing.'
(a) Name the fuel and the source of oxygen already there.
(b) Say what the lens supplies and how.
questions.a: (a) The paper is the fuel and the air supplies the oxygen. (b) It supplies heat: focused sunrays raise the paper's temperature until it reaches its ignition temperature.
s: paper as fuel and air as oxygen
heat from focused sunrays raising it to the ignition temperature

questions.q:
A fire-safety rule says, 'Do not stack paper near a burning lamp, even if the flame does not touch it.'
(a) Which requirement of burning could the lamp's heat provide?
(b) What must happen to the paper's temperature before it burns?
questions.a: (a) Heat. (b) Its temperature must rise to the ignition temperature of paper, the minimum temperature at which it catches fire.
s: the lamp provides heat
the paper must reach its ignition temperature

questions.q:
A wax candle is burning on a table.
(a) Name the fuel, the source of oxygen and the source of heat.
(b) A tumbler is placed over it. Which of the three is cut off?
questions.a: (a) Wax (its vapour) is the fuel, air gives the oxygen, and the flame gives the heat. (b) The supply of oxygen (air) is cut off, so the flame goes out.
s: wax, air and flame named
the tumbler cuts off oxygen

questions.q:
A fire-safety card gives two rules: (i) wrap a cotton blanket round a person whose clothes are on fire; (ii) keep paper away from lamps and stoves.
(a) Which side of the fire triangle does each rule deal with?
(b) Which rule prevents a fire from starting and which stops one that has started?
questions.a: (a) Rule (i) cuts off the oxygen; rule (ii) keeps heat away so the paper cannot reach its ignition temperature. (b) Rule (ii) prevents a fire; rule (i) stops a fire already burning.
s: blanket removes oxygen; keeping paper away removes heat
(ii) prevents, (i) stops a fire in progress

questions.q: Kavya says: 'A substance can burn without a flame touching it.' Is she right? What more must she add to be complete?
questions.a: Yes: paper burns under focused sunrays with no flame near it. To be complete she must add that the substance needs oxygen and must be heated to its ignition temperature.
s: verdict: yes, with the sunray example
oxygen is needed
it must be heated to its ignition temperature

questions.q: Write a three-line situation in which a fire is stopped by removing exactly one side of the fire triangle. Name the side removed and the two sides that were still present.
questions.a: e.g. Burning clothes are smothered with a cotton blanket, which cuts off the air, so the fire stops. The fuel (cloth) and the heat were still present.
s: situation with an action that stops the fire
side removed named with reason
the other two sides named as still present

questions.q: Rahul wants to put out a burning sheet of paper by 'taking away its ignition temperature'. Show that this cannot be done and say what can be changed instead.
questions.a: The ignition temperature is the minimum temperature at which that substance catches fire; it belongs to the substance and cannot be taken away. What can be changed is the paper's own temperature, which can be kept below the ignition temperature by removing heat, or the fire can be stopped by removing oxygen or fuel.
s: ignition temperature is a property of the substance
cannot be removed
what can be changed: heat, oxygen or fuel

questions.q:
Four trials with paper or a stone: (i) a sheet of paper kept on a desk in the open; (ii) a stone held near a lighted matchstick; (iii) a sheet of paper held to a lighted matchstick; (iv) a sheet of paper held in a flame inside a sealed jar whose oxygen is all used up.
(a) Predict whether a fire starts in each.
(b) Name the missing side of the fire triangle in each trial without a fire.
(c) State what the trial with a fire has.
questions.a: (a) Only trial (iii) gives a fire. (b) (i) heat; (ii) fuel; (iv) oxygen. (c) Trial (iii) has fuel (paper), oxygen (air) and heat from a match hotter than the paper's ignition temperature.
s: prediction for all four trials
heat missing in (i)
fuel missing in (ii) and oxygen missing in (iv)
trial (iii) has all three sides

questions.q:
A student heats a sheet of paper with focused sunrays and records its temperature: at 0 s it is 30 degrees C, at 30 s 60, at 60 s 90, at 90 s 120, at 120 s 150 and at 150 s 180, when it catches fire. Assume the paper's ignition temperature is 180 degrees C and the temperature keeps rising at the same steady rate.
(a) Find the rate of rise in degrees C per second.
(b) Name the temperature at which the paper caught fire and say why a lighted match sets the same paper on fire almost at once.
(c) She moves the lens away at 100 s. Find the temperature then and say whether the paper catches fire.
questions.a: (a) 30 degrees per 30 s = 1 degree C per second. (b) The ignition temperature; the match is already hotter than it, so the paper reaches it almost immediately. (c) 30 + 100 = 130 degrees C, below 180, so the paper does not catch fire.
s: rate 1 degree C per second
name: ignition temperature
match already hotter than the ignition temperature
temperature 130 degrees C at 100 s
below 180, so no fire

questions.q:
A kadhai of oil on a gas stove catches fire in the school canteen. The cook switches off the stove and covers the kadhai with a metal lid, and the flame goes out. After 10 seconds a helper lifts the lid to check and the flame returns. The oil was at 340 degrees C when the lid went on and cools by 10 degrees C every 20 seconds under the lid. The ignition temperature of this oil is 300 degrees C.
(a) Which side of the fire triangle did the lid remove, and which two remained?
(b) Why did the flame return?
(c) After how many seconds under the lid does the oil first cool to 300 degrees C?
(d) Decide when the helper should lift the lid and justify.
questions.a: (a) Oxygen was removed; fuel (oil) and heat remained. (b) Air entered when the lid was lifted and the oil, at about 335 degrees C, was still above its ignition temperature. (c) 40 / 10 x 20 = 80 seconds. (d) Not before the oil has cooled to its ignition temperature, 80 seconds, and preferably longer, so that when air returns the oil cannot catch fire.
s: oxygen removed; fuel and heat remained
air returned while oil was above its ignition temperature
80 seconds
lift only after the oil is below the ignition temperature

questions.q:
On a camping trip, students have three matches, a sheet of paper, a handful of dry twigs and one big log. A match flame lasts about 20 seconds. The ignition temperature is lowest for paper, higher for the twigs and highest for the log. Plan P: hold a match straight to the log. Plan Q: light the paper, set it under the twigs, and let the twigs heat the log.
(a) Why does a match set the paper alight almost at once?
(b) Why may the match fail to light the log within its 20 seconds?
(c) What does the burning paper give to the twigs, and the burning twigs to the log?
(d) Decide between Plan P and Plan Q and justify.
questions.a: (a) The match is already hotter than the paper's ignition temperature. (b) The log has the highest ignition temperature and the match cannot supply enough heat to raise it that high in the time. (c) Heat, to bring them to their ignition temperatures. (d) Plan Q: each fuel supplies the heat to bring the next one to its ignition temperature, which a single match cannot do for the log.
s: match hotter than the ignition temperature of paper
log needs more heat than a 20 s match gives
heat passed on to the next fuel
Plan Q chosen with reason

questions.q: Zara watches a candle in a lantern and notes five things in order: (P) wax near the wick melts, (Q) liquid wax climbs the wick, (R) wax at the top turns to vapour, (S) a yellow flame appears, (T) wax drops harden at the base. Which pair are physical changes that happen BEFORE the flame forms?
questions.a: P and R: melting, then vaporisation, both physical. The flame (S) is the burning of the vapour, a chemical change, so each other pair includes it.
o: P and R
P and S
R and S
Q and S

questions.q: Which single observation at a lit candle is the best evidence that a chemical change, and not only a physical one, is going on?
questions.a: The flame is the burning of wax vapour, which forms new substances. The other three are melting, solidifying and movement of melted wax, which are physical.
o: A yellow flame at the wick tip, where the vapour of wax burns
Wax near the wick turns to a clear liquid and gathers in a small pool
Drops of wax run down the side and harden into white beads at the base
Melted wax travels up the wick towards the heat of the flame above

questions.q: Imran says, 'The flame of a candle is produced by the wick alone.' Which statement corrects him best?
questions.a: Wax melts, is carried up the wick and evaporates; the vapour of wax burns to give the flame.
o: The flame is the burning of wax vapour; the wick only carries melted wax upwards
The flame is the burning of solid wax at the base; the wick only holds it up
The flame is the evaporation of wax, a physical change, and the wick feeds it air
The flame appears when melted wax hardens again on the wick, giving off light

questions.q: Mansi collects the hard wax drips from a burning candle and melts them to make a small new candle. Her friend asks, 'Can you also make a candle from the wax that burned?' Which reply is correct?
questions.a: Melting and setting are physical changes that can be reversed. Burning of the vapour forms new substances, so the burnt wax is not wax any more.
o: No: the drips only melted and set, but the burnt wax formed new substances
Yes: all the wax is the same material, so the burnt wax can be melted again too
No: both the drips and the burnt wax went through chemical changes and cannot be reversed
Yes: the burnt wax turned to vapour, and vapour can be condensed back into the same wax

questions.q: A teacher has one cheap object and wants a single demonstration that shows both physical and chemical changes, as Faraday used in his lectures. Which object should she choose?
questions.a: A candle shows melting, evaporation and solidifying (physical) and the burning of vapour (chemical). The ice cube and the folded paper show only physical changes; the magnesium ribbon shows mainly the chemical change of burning.
o: A candle
An ice cube
A sheet of paper to be folded
A magnesium ribbon

questions.q:
Read the statements about a burning candle.
I. The wick burns as the fuel while the wax only supports it.
II. The melting and the solidifying of wax are physical changes.
III. The burning of wax vapour is a physical change because the wax is still wax afterwards.
questions.a: I is false: the wax vapour is the fuel and the wick carries melted wax. III is false: burning forms new substances. II is true.
o: II only
I only
III only
I and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A candle burning inside a closed lantern with no air vents goes out sooner than one in an open lantern.
Reason (R): The burning of wax vapour is a chemical change that needs oxygen from the air.
questions.a: Both are true. Combustion needs a continuing supply of oxygen, and a closed lantern cannot give it, so R explains A.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

questions.q: A student notes one event each minute at a candle. Minute 1: wax melts. Minute 2: wax evaporates. Minute 3: vapour burns. Minute 4: wax drops harden. Minute 5: vapour burns again. The number of minutes in which a chemical change is noted is ___.
True or False? Give the reason or the correction. 'The wax drops that run down a lit candle and harden at its base are new substances formed by the burning.'
questions.a: False. The drops are wax that melted and set again. This is a physical change; no new substance is formed, and the hardened wax can be melted again.
s: verdict: false
correction: melting and solidifying are physical, the drops are still wax

questions.q:
Compare two things the wax of a candle goes through: (i) dripping and hardening at the base, (ii) the burning of wax vapour at the wick.
(a) For each, say whether a new substance forms.
(b) For each, say whether the material can be got back as wax by melting.
questions.a: (a) (i) No new substance; (ii) new substances form. (b) (i) Yes, the hardened wax can be melted again; (ii) No, the wax that burned is no longer wax.
s: no new substance in (i), new substances in (ii)
(i) can be melted again; (ii) cannot be got back as wax

questions.q:
Priya writes the stages of a burning candle as: wax burns, then melts, then evaporates.
(a) Correct the order.
(b) Say which stage is the chemical change.
questions.a: (a) Wax melts, is carried up the wick, evaporates, and then the vapour burns. (b) The burning of the vapour.
s: correct order: melts, rises, evaporates, vapour burns
burning of the vapour is chemical

questions.q:
When a candle burns, carbon dioxide forms from the carbon in the wax and the oxygen of the air.
(a) At which step of the candle's burning does the carbon dioxide form?
(b) Would carbon dioxide form if the wax only melted and evaporated without being lit? Explain.
questions.a: (a) When the wax vapour burns, which is a chemical change. (b) No: melting and evaporation are physical changes in which no new substance is formed.
s: carbon dioxide forms as the vapour burns
no, melting and evaporation form no new substance

questions.q:
Neha says, 'The wax near the wick disappears by evaporating, so evaporation is a chemical change.'
(a) Do you agree?
(b) What does she need to see to call a change at the candle chemical?
questions.a: (a) No. Evaporation is a physical change: the wax only changes state from liquid to vapour. (b) A new substance being formed, as when the vapour burns with heat and light.
s: evaporation is physical, a change of state
a new substance, as in burning of the vapour

questions.q: Sunil says: 'A candle gets shorter only because its wax melts and drips down; nothing is burnt away.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. If the candle got shorter only through dripping, there would be no flame. The melted wax is carried up the wick and evaporates, and its vapour burns to form new substances, so part of the wax is burnt away as well as dripping.
s: verdict: no
wax also evaporates and its vapour burns
burning forms new substances, so that wax is burnt away

questions.q: A card set reads: physical, physical, chemical. Write one thing seen at a lit candle for each card, in the order in which the three happen.
questions.a: e.g. Physical: wax near the wick melts into a clear liquid. Physical: the liquid wax rises up the wick and evaporates in the heat. Chemical: the vapour burns as a yellow flame, giving light and heat.
s: a physical change seen first
a second physical change after it
the chemical change last, with the flame

questions.q: Show that melting and evaporation alone cannot produce the flame of a candle.
questions.a: Melting and evaporation are physical changes in which only the state of wax changes and no new substance is formed. The flame is light and heat from the burning of wax vapour, a chemical change that forms new substances, so something more than a change of state is needed.
s: melting and evaporation are state changes with no new substance
the flame is the burning of the vapour
burning is a chemical change, so melting and evaporation alone are not enough

questions.q:
Your class runs a 'Candle Detective' stall at the school fair. Visitors watch a lit candle for five minutes.
(a) Write a four-step script of what a visitor sees, in order, and label each step physical or chemical.
(b) A visitor says, 'The candle melts, so burning a candle is only a physical change.' Write the stall's reply.
questions.a: (a) Wax near the wick melts (physical); the melted wax is carried up the wick and evaporates (physical); the vapour burns as the flame (chemical); wax drops run down and harden at the base (physical). (b) Melting is physical, but the burning of the vapour forms new substances, so the candle shows both kinds of change.
s: steps in correct order
melting, evaporation and hardening labelled physical
burning of the vapour labelled chemical
reply accepts melting is physical
reply gives the burning of the vapour as the chemical change

questions.q:
Complete this table for four events and then answer the question. Events: (E1) an ice cube melting in the sun; (E2) a magnesium ribbon burning in air; (E3) wax melting near a candle wick; (E4) wax vapour burning at the wick.
(a) For each event, say whether a new substance is formed.
(b) For each event, say whether it is physical or chemical.
(c) Say which events give out heat and light.
(d) Which of E1 and E2 matches each of the two kinds of change shown by E3 and E4, and what does this say about a candle?
questions.a: (a) E1 no; E2 yes (magnesium oxide); E3 no; E4 yes. (b) E1 and E3 physical; E2 and E4 chemical. (c) E2 and E4 give out heat and light. (d) E1 matches E3 (physical melting) and E2 matches E4 (chemical burning). A candle has both kinds of change in one process.
s: new substance in E2 and E4 only
E1 and E3 physical; E2 and E4 chemical
heat and light from E2 and E4
melting events grouped and burning events grouped
candle involves both kinds of change

questions.q:
During a class activity three groups watch a lit candle for five minutes and note one thing each. Group P: wax near the wick turns into a clear liquid. Group Q: a yellow flame sits at the tip of the wick, and the wax near the wick slowly disappears. Group R: drops run down the sides and become a white solid at the base.
(a) Name the change P noted and its type.
(b) What exactly burns in the flame Q saw, and what type of change is it?
(c) Name the change R noted and its type.
(d) Two groups argue over whether burning a candle is physical or chemical. Decide, naming which groups' notes support each side.
questions.a: (a) Melting, physical. (b) Wax vapour; chemical. (c) Solidifying, physical. (d) Both: P and R support physical, Q supports chemical, so a candle shows both kinds of change.
s: melting, physical
wax vapour burns, chemical
solidifying, physical
both kinds, with P and R physical and Q chemical

questions.q:
Sneha lit a wax candle in a lantern on Diwali night. The candle weighed 40 g to begin with and 28 g after three hours, and the ring of hard wax that had dripped and set at its base weighed 5 g. Her brother wants to collect the hard wax and melt it to make a new candle. Her mother says burning a candle is completely reversible, so no wax is lost. Assume that all the wax that left the wick as vapour was burnt.
(a) Name the physical changes that the wax went through.
(b) Work out the mass of wax that was burnt.
(c) What kind of change was the burning, and what did it form?
(d) Decide whether the mother is right and say how much wax can be reused.
questions.a: (a) Melting, evaporation and solidifying. (b) 40 - 28 - 5 = 7 g. (c) A chemical change, forming new substances (such as carbon dioxide). (d) Mother is wrong: the 5 g of hard wax can be remelted, but the 7 g that burned formed new substances and cannot be got back as wax.
s: melting, evaporation and solidifying
7 g burnt
chemical change forming new substances
5 g reusable, 7 g not; mother wrong

questions.q: In a hostel kitchen the cook lets steam from boiling rice condense into droplets on the lid, chops onions for the curry, pops some corn for the evening snack and leaves ice cubes to melt in a glass. Which pair of these changes includes two that can BOTH be reversed?
questions.a: Steam condensing back to water and ice refrozen are reversible. Chopped onions and popped corn cannot go back, so every other pair is mixed or both irreversible.
o: Steam condensing on the lid; ice melting in the glass
Steam condensing on the lid; onions being chopped up
Onions being chopped up; corn being popped for a snack
Corn being popped for a snack; ice melting in the glass

questions.q: A town wants to slow the rise of carbon dioxide in its air that the chapter links to human activity. Which step helps most directly?
questions.a: More fuel burnt in vehicles raises the carbon dioxide in the air. Painting less reduces the substances released as paint dries, which is a different effect.
o: Burning less petrol and diesel
Repainting the public walls less often than now
Cutting vegetables into smaller pieces
Keeping ice frozen for longer hours

questions.q: Which pair of changes is BOTH physical AND can be reversed?
questions.a: Melting and evaporation are changes of state, physical, and both can be reversed by freezing and condensing. Chopped vegetables cannot be got back and rusting forms a new substance.
o: Melting of ice; evaporation of water
Chopping of vegetables; melting of ice
Rusting of iron; melting of ice
Chopping of vegetables; evaporation of water

questions.q: The chapter lists 'boiling water in an open pan' among changes you may be unsure about as reversible or not. Which reason best explains the doubt?
questions.a: Water that evaporates can be condensed back into liquid water, but in an open pan the vapour mixes with the air, so getting all of it back is doubtful.
o: Steam spreads into the open air, so it is hard to condense all of it back
Boiling forms a new substance, so the water cannot be got back at all
Steam is a different substance from water, so it cannot turn back into water
Water can be heated only once, so a second boiling is not possible

questions.q:
Read the statements about changes around us.
I. Burning more petrol and diesel in vehicles adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
II. Melting of ice and making of popcorn are both changes that can be reversed.
III. Drying paint harms the air by releasing substances through condensation.
questions.a: II is false: popcorn cannot be changed back into corn. III is false: the substances are released through evaporation. I is true.
o: I only
II only
III only
I and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Melting of ice is a reversible change.
Reason (R): Popcorn cannot be changed back into corn.
questions.a: Both are true. R is another fact about reversibility, but it describes an irreversible change and does not explain why ice can be refrozen.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

questions.q: A cook lets ice cubes melt in a glass, chops vegetables, pops corn and lets steam condense on a lid. If she tries to get back the original in each case, the number of changes she can reverse is ___.

Match Column I with Column II.
1. Ice melting in a glass
2. Cutting fruits for a salad
3. Food waste decaying in a garden pit
4. More petrol and diesel vehicles on the road
A. Adds carbon dioxide to the atmosphere
B. Can be reversed by freezing again
C. Undesirable in storage, but useful as compost
D. Desirable, though it cannot be reversed
questions.a: Melting ice: reversible (B); cutting fruits: desirable but not reversible (D); decay of waste: useful as compost (C); more vehicles: more carbon dioxide (A).

questions.q: True or False? Give the reason or the correction. 'A cut fruit cannot be made whole again, yet the cutting of fruits is counted as a desirable change.'
questions.a: True. Whether a change can be reversed and whether it is desirable are separate questions; cutting fruits is useful although it cannot be undone.
s: verdict: true
reason: reversibility and desirability are independent

questions.q:
Cutting of fruits and rusting of iron are both changes that cannot be reversed.
(a) Say which of the two the chapter calls desirable and which undesirable.
(b) What does this show about the two ways of grouping changes?
questions.a: (a) Cutting of fruits is desirable; rusting of iron is undesirable. (b) Grouping by reversible or not is separate from grouping by desirable or not; an irreversible change can be either.
s: cutting desirable, rusting undesirable
the two groupings are independent

questions.q:
A delivery van burns 6 litres of petrol a day for 30 days.
(a) How many litres does it burn in the 30 days?
(b) Name the gas whose amount in the atmosphere rises because of such burning and say what kind of change burning is.
questions.a: (a) 6 x 30 = 180 litres. (b) Carbon dioxide; burning fuel is a chemical change (combustion).
s: 180 litres
carbon dioxide; burning is a chemical change

questions.q:
A school campaign says: 'Repaint classrooms every four years instead of every two to cut atmospheric pollution.'
(a) Which effect of painting does this aim at?
(b) Explain, using the chapter, why repainting less often helps.
questions.a: (a) Pollution of the air by the substances released when paint dries. (b) Drying of paint releases many substances through evaporation; painting half as often means fewer such releases.
s: pollution from the substances released as paint dries
drying releases substances by evaporation, so less painting releases less

questions.q:
Anil says, 'Chopped vegetables can be cooked, so chopping is a reversible change.'
(a) Point out his mistake.
(b) State what cannot be got back after chopping.
questions.a: (a) Cooking is a different change; it does not bring the vegetables back to their uncut form. (b) The original size and shape.
s: cooking is another change, not the reversal of chopping
original size and shape cannot be got back

questions.q: Ruchi says: 'Human activity changes the environment only by burning fuels.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: Partly right. Burning more fuel in cars, trains and aeroplanes does raise the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. But it is not the only way: drying of paint on walls and furniture releases substances through evaporation and pollutes the air.
s: verdict: partly right
burning fuel raises carbon dioxide
drying paint is another cause, so 'only' is wrong

questions.q: Write a three-line notice for a society's board that includes one change that can be reversed, one that cannot, and one that is desirable in one place and undesirable in another. Name the place for each side of the last one.
questions.a: e.g. Ice cubes in a glass can be refrozen. Cut vegetables cannot be made whole again. Food waste decays: bad in the store room, but useful in the garden pit as compost.
s: a reversible change named
an irreversible change named
decay with the two places named

questions.q: Draw up a three-point plan for your school to reduce the long-term effect of human activity on the environment. Link each point to a cause named in the chapter.
questions.a: e.g. 1. Share rides or cycle to burn less petrol and diesel (burning fuel raises carbon dioxide). 2. Repaint walls less often (drying paint releases substances by evaporation). 3. Turn canteen waste into compost instead of letting it spoil (useful decay).
s: a point on burning less fuel with its cause
a point on painting with its cause
a third point linked to a cause in the chapter

questions.q:
A society has four things: (i) kitchen waste in a pit; (ii) an iron gate that is rusting; (iii) milk turning into curd at the dairy stall; (iv) food spoiling on a shelf.
(a) Classify each as desirable or undesirable.
(b) Which two are the same kind of change but need opposite decisions?
(c) Which undesirable change in the list is not a form of decay?
(d) The society decides to stop the decay in (iv). Should it stop the decay in (i) too? Justify.
questions.a: (a) (i) desirable, (ii) undesirable, (iii) desirable, (iv) undesirable. (b) (i) and (iv), both decay. (c) Rusting of the gate. (d) No: in the pit the decay turns waste into compost, which is useful, while on the shelf it spoils food.
s: all four classified correctly
(i) and (iv) as the pair of decay
rusting is the undesirable change that is not decay
do not stop (i): decay gives compost

questions.q:
A student's table for 'Can the original be got back?' reads: melting ice cubes - Yes; chopping vegetables - Yes; boiling water and cooling the steam on a cold lid - Yes; making popcorn from corn - Yes.
(a) Identify the two wrong entries.
(b) Correct each and give the reason from the chapter.
(c) A friend says every 'No' in the table is a chemical change. Show with one entry that she is wrong.
questions.a: (a) Chopping vegetables and making popcorn. (b) Chopped vegetables cannot return to their original size and shape, so No. Popcorn cannot go back to its original form, so No. (c) Chopping vegetables is a physical change (no new substance) although it cannot be reversed.
s: the two wrong entries identified
chopping corrected to No with reason
popcorn corrected to No with reason
chopping is a physical change that is not reversible

questions.q:
In Meenakshi's housing society, kitchen waste is put in a pit at the back of the compound and, after some weeks, is used as compost for the garden. Residents of the nearest block complain about the smell from the pit. The iron gate has brown patches, and food kept in the hall's storage room spoiled last month.
(a) Is the change in the pit desirable or undesirable? Explain.
(b) Name the change on the gate.
(c) Why is the spoilage in the storage room undesirable though the same decay is useful in the pit?
(d) The secretary must choose: keep the pit but move it away from houses, or close it and send waste away. Decide.
questions.a: (a) Desirable: waste becomes compost. (b) Rusting; undesirable. (c) The food is wasted in storage; in the pit it is used. (d) Keep the pit but move it, to keep the useful change and reduce the smell.
s: desirable: waste becomes compost
rusting, undesirable
same decay, different situation
move the pit, keeping the useful change

questions.q:
Aman uses 4 litres of petrol a week on his scooter. Petrol costs Rs 105 a litre. The wall of his shop is repainted every two years at Rs 12,000 each time. He can cycle to the shop instead of riding, which saves all of the 4 litres a week, or he can repaint every four years instead of two. Time allows him to do only one of the two.
(a) How many litres of petrol does he burn in a year of 52 weeks?
(b) How much money does cycling save in a year?
(c) How much money a year does repainting every four years save?
(d) Decide which one he should choose, naming the effect on the air that each avoids.
questions.a: (a) 4 x 52 = 208 litres. (b) 208 x 105 = Rs 21,840. (c) 12,000 / 2 = 6,000 a year now and 12,000 / 4 = 3,000 a year later, a saving of Rs 3,000. (d) Cycling: it saves Rs 18,840 more a year and avoids carbon dioxide from burning fuel; repainting less would only avoid the substances released as paint dries.
s: 208 litres
Rs 3,000 a year
cycling chosen, with the effect each avoids

questions.q: On a hill, a trekker finds (P) a black rock with a red crust on its surface and (Q) a heap of sand and stones at the foot of the cliff. Which pair of explanations fits best?
questions.a: The red layer on iron-containing basalt is iron oxide, a chemical change from water or moist air. The heap of sand and stones comes from physical breaking of the rock.
o: P: moist air reacted with the iron in the rock, a chemical change; Q: the cliff rock broke up by physical changes
P: the rock broke into red pieces, a physical change of size; Q: the cliff rock reacted with water in a chemical change
P: wind blew red soil onto the rock, which is erosion; Q: the rock changed chemically into sand over the years
P and Q: both physical changes, since a change of colour never shows that a new substance has formed

questions.q: Water seeps into a crack in a boulder on a cold mountain, freezes, and widens the crack until the boulder splits. Which description is correct?
questions.a: Freezing of water in cracks is a cause of the physical breaking of rock, which is weathering. Erosion is the moving of material by wind and flowing water.
o: Weathering, a physical change because no new substance forms
Erosion, a physical change because the pieces are moved away
Weathering, a chemical change because the water reacts with the rock
Erosion, a chemical change because the rock is broken up for good

questions.q: A hill stream carries sand and silt into a wide lake. In this journey the rock breaks, the pieces are carried, the pieces settle, and the sediments harden. Which stage happens because the water slows down?
questions.a: Material carried by water settles when the speed of the water decreases, as in a lake. Hardening takes thousands of years.
o: The pieces settle at the lake bottom
The rock breaks into smaller pieces on the slope
The pieces are carried along by the stream
The sediments harden into new rock over time

questions.q: Four events: (i) a black iron-containing rock gets a red layer after years in damp air; (ii) tree roots widen a crack in a rock; (iii) a landslide carries earth downhill; (iv) a stream rolls pebbles until they are smooth. Which are physical changes?
questions.a: Event (i) forms iron oxide, a chemical change. Roots breaking rock, a landslide and a stream smoothing pebbles form no new substance, so they are physical.
o: (ii), (iii) and (iv)
(i), (ii) and (iii)
(i), (iii) and (iv)
(i), (ii), (iii) and (iv)

questions.q: Pebbles taken from a river close to its spring are rough, while pebbles taken far downstream are smoother. Which explanation fits the chapter?
questions.a: River rocks and pebbles are smoother because of the constant erosion caused by flowing water, a physical change.
o: The downstream pebbles have been rubbed for longer by flowing water, which is erosion
The downstream pebbles were chemically changed by the river into a different new substance
The spring pebbles are the ones that have already been hardened into new rock
The river adds a smooth coating of iron oxide to every pebble that it carries along

questions.q:
Read the statements about rocks.
I. Weathering of rocks involves only physical changes.
II. The red colour on basalt is due to iron oxide formed by a physical change.
III. Erosion by wind or flowing water is a chemical change.
questions.a: I is false: weathering has physical and chemical changes. II is false: iron oxide forms by a chemical change. III is false: erosion is a physical change. So none is correct.
o: None of the three
I only
II and III only
I and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Erosion by flowing water is a physical change.
Reason (R): Erosion converts rocks into soil by a chemical reaction with water.
questions.a: A is true. R is false: the formation of soil from rocks is weathering; erosion only breaks down and moves material.
o: Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

questions.q: A lake bed receives 1.5 cm of sediment each year. At that steady rate, a layer 60 cm thick takes ___ years to settle.

Match Column I with Column II.
1. Tree roots widen a crack in a boulder
2. Black basalt turns red after years in moist air
3. A river carries silt downstream
4. Silt settles in a lake and sets over thousands of years
A. Erosion by flowing water
B. New rock forms and the change cannot be reversed
C. Physical weathering
D. Chemical weathering
questions.a: Roots: physical weathering (C); basalt turning red: chemical weathering (D); river carrying silt: erosion (A); settling and hardening: new rock, not reversible (B).

questions.q: True or False? Give the reason or the correction. 'Erosion during a landslide is a chemical change because the rock is destroyed.'
questions.a: False. A landslide only breaks up and moves earth and rock from one place to another; no new substance is formed, so erosion is a physical change.
s: verdict: false
correction: erosion is a physical change, no new substance forms

questions.q:
Kiran looks at a black rock with a red surface layer and says, 'Only the colour has changed, so it is a physical change.'
(a) Name the red substance.
(b) Say why his reasoning fails.
questions.a: (a) Iron oxide. (b) A colour change can come from a new substance forming; the iron in the rock reacted with water or moist air, which is a chemical change.
s: iron oxide
a new substance formed, so the change is chemical

questions.q:
After a heavy shower, a farmer finds that a stream of muddy water has carried soil from the top of his sloping field to a pond at the bottom.
(a) Name the process that moved the soil.
(b) Say what type of change it is and why.
questions.a: (a) Erosion by flowing water. (b) A physical change: the soil is only moved from one place to another and no new substance forms.
s: erosion by flowing water
physical, no new substance

questions.q:
Along a river, Spot X is a narrow steep gorge where the water rushes and Spot Y is where the river enters a wide lake.
(a) At which spot do the sediments settle?
(b) Give the reason and say what the sediments can become in time.
questions.a: (a) At Spot Y. (b) Material settles when the speed of the water decreases; over thousands of years the sediments harden into new rocks.
s: spot Y, the lake
water slows; sediments harden to rock over a long time

questions.a: (a) Weathering breaks and changes rocks where they are, and leads to soil; erosion breaks down and moves rock, pebbles and soil by wind and flowing water. (b) Weathering, e.g. black basalt with iron forming red iron oxide.
s: weathering changes rock in place; erosion moves material
weathering has chemical changes, e.g. basalt turning red

questions.q: Dev says: 'A mountain stream that rolls pebbles for years makes them smoother, and this smoothing is a physical change.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes. River rocks and pebbles become smoother because of the constant erosion by flowing water. Only the shape and surface change; the pebbles remain the same substance, so no new substance forms and it is physical.
s: verdict: yes
constant erosion by flowing water smooths them
no new substance, so physical

questions.q: Write a three-line situation in which one rock is acted on by both a physical and a chemical change. Name the cause of each.
questions.a: e.g. A black rock on a hill has roots of a tree growing in its cracks, which break it (physical). Its surface turns red after years in damp air because the iron in it forms iron oxide (chemical).
s: one rock in one situation
physical change with its cause
chemical change with its cause

questions.q: Explain in three linked steps how the sediments at the bottom of a lake can become a new rock, and say why this cannot be quickly reversed.
