questions.a: Pieces of rock, soil and sand are moved by flowing water; when the water slows in the lake they settle at the bottom; they harden over thousands of years into new rocks. Because this takes thousands of years, the change cannot be reversed.
s: pieces carried by flowing water
settle when the water slows, then harden over a long time
takes thousands of years, so not reversible

questions.q:
A student collects three samples from a hilly area: S1 is loose sand and stones from the foot of a cliff; S2 is a black rock with a red surface layer; S3 is a smooth round pebble from a river bed.
(a) For each sample, name the process that produced it (weathering or erosion) and say whether the change is physical or chemical.
(b) Name the substance that makes S2 red.
(c) Which two samples show physical changes only?
questions.a: (a) S1: weathering, physical breaking of the cliff rock. S2: weathering, chemical change. S3: erosion by flowing water, physical. (b) Iron oxide. (c) S1 and S3.
s: S1 weathering, physical
S2 weathering, chemical
S3 erosion, physical
iron oxide
S1 and S3 physical only

questions.q:
A geology student studies a lake shore. Layer 3 at the top is loose silt just settled. Layer 2 below is thin bands of fine sand and silt, slightly hardened. On the hill above, boulders have cracks with tree roots growing in them, and a black rock has a red crust.
(a) Explain how the silt of layer 3 got to the lake.
(b) What will happen to layer 3 over thousands of years?
(c) Which observations on the hill show weathering, and of which type?
(d) A visitor says layer 2 can be turned back into the hill boulders. Evaluate.
questions.a: (a) Erosion by flowing water carried the broken material, which settled when the water slowed in the lake. (b) It will harden into new rock. (c) Roots in the cracks show physical weathering; the red crust of iron oxide shows chemical weathering. (d) Not possible: these changes take thousands of years and cannot be reversed.
s: erosion by flowing water; settles as water slows
hardens into new rock
roots: physical; red crust: chemical
cannot be reversed

questions.q:
A hill stream carries brown water into a village reservoir. Silt settles on the floor of the reservoir at 2.5 cm a year. The water intake pipe is 90 cm above the floor. The village committee wonders whether to dredge the silt out before it reaches the pipe or to wait for it to turn into rock and stay out of the way.
(a) Name the process that carried the soil to the reservoir.
(b) Why does the silt settle in the reservoir and not in the fast stream?
(c) In how many years will the silt reach the intake pipe?
(d) Decide whether to dredge or to wait, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Erosion by flowing water. (b) In the reservoir the water slows, and material settles when the speed of the water decreases. (c) 90 / 2.5 = 36 years. (d) Dredge before 36 years: silt hardens into rock only over thousands of years, so in 36 years it will still be loose silt blocking the intake.
s: erosion by flowing water
water slows in the reservoir
36 years
dredge, as hardening takes thousands of years

questions.q:
On a trip to the Uttarakhand foothills, students found sand, soil and stones at the base of a steep slope. The guide showed a black rock with a red layer on its surface, and said a landslide after heavy rain had moved earth downhill. In the nearby river they found smooth round pebbles. The class can collect samples from only one place, either the base of the cliff or the riverbed, to show the effect of long, constant erosion by flowing water.
(a) How were the sand and stones at the base formed?
(b) Name the substance in the red layer and the type of change.
(c) What do we call the movement of earth in the landslide, and what kind of change is it?
(d) Decide which place gives the better samples and why.
questions.a: (a) Large rocks broke by physical changes. (b) Iron oxide; chemical. (c) Erosion; physical. (d) The riverbed: its smooth pebbles result from constant erosion by flowing water, while the cliff base shows weathering and a landslide.
s: large rocks broke by physical changes
iron oxide; chemical
erosion; physical
riverbed: smooth pebbles from constant erosion
